items.title: Module 22 Opener, Encounter the Phenomenon and CER: How could controlling the quantum states of individual atoms be useful for building extremely accurate clocks?

body.html: This is an open-ended claim-evidence-reasoning prompt. Nothing is calculated.

Atoms have quantized energy levels. Every atom of one kind has exactly the same energy gap between two particular levels, so it absorbs or emits light of exactly one frequency, 𝑓= 𝛥𝐸/ ℎ. A clock needs a steady, repeatable "tick", and that frequency can be the tick.

A reasonable claim is "Locking a light source to the transition frequency of an atom gives a clock whose ticks are identical everywhere." Evidence to collect from this module: (1) energy is quantized, so atoms of the same element have identical, repeatable energy gaps; (2) a photon emitted in a jump carries energy 𝐸= ℎ𝑓, so the gap sets an exact frequency (for example, a 2.10 eV gap gives 𝑓= 𝐸/ ℎ= 5.1 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz); (3) emission and absorption spectra show that the lines are narrow and sit at the same wavelengths every time. Reasoning: because a transition frequency is fixed by the atom and not by the clock's construction, counting cycles of light locked to it gives a time standard that does not drift.

answer.html: Sample claim: the fixed, quantized energy gaps of atoms give an exact light frequency that can be counted as a very stable clock tick. (Student-specific wording will vary.)

items.title: Unit 6 Opener, Ask Questions, Look for Evidence, and STEM Project: How did the chemical elements around us come to exist?

body.html: Open-ended prompts: write questions for the board, record observations in a Summary Table, and plan a research timeline using online resources.
These tasks are student-generated and use online resources, so no single numerical result exists. Here is a model response.

Sample questions: Where did hydrogen and helium come from? How do stars make heavier elements? How do we know which elements are in a distant star? What happens to the elements when a star dies? Summary Table headings: Activity | Observation | Explanation | Connection to the unit question. A sample entry from this module: the bright-line spectrum of a gas matches the line pattern of one element, so spectra let us read the elements in a star from its light. For the STEM project, gather evidence such as the abundance of hydrogen and helium in the universe, element lines in starlight, and supernova remnants, and then arrange them in a timeline.

answer.html: Not a computed problem. Sample questions and a Summary Table format are given above; the unit project needs the online resources, so only the method is shown here.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 1 and 2): A blacksmith heats an iron bar in a forge, and the bar changes from dull red to orange to yellow-white. Explain the changes in color and brightness as its temperature rises.

body.html: The bar's temperature increases. We need to explain why the color changes and why the bar gets brighter.
A hotter object has an emission spectrum that peaks at a higher frequency, and it emits more total power (proportional to 𝑇<sup>4</sup>).

At lower temperature the peak of the spectrum is in the infrared, and only the long-wavelength red edge reaches the visible range, so the bar glows a dull red. As the temperature rises, the peak moves to higher frequency, so orange, yellow and then shorter wavelengths are added. When many colors are present in similar amounts, the eye sees yellow-white. The total power emitted also grows quickly, so the bar is much brighter.

answer.html: As the bar heats up, its spectrum peak shifts to higher frequency (dull red, to orange, to yellow-white) and it emits more total power, so it glows brighter.

check.html: A very hot bar looks white and bright, while a barely hot bar looks dim and red, which agrees with this explanation.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Astronomy Connection): A star's surface temperature changes from 4000 K to 6000 K. By what factor does the power it radiates per unit area change?

body.html: 𝑃∝𝑇<sup>4</sup>, with 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 4000 K and 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 6000 K. Find 𝑃<sub>2</sub> / 𝑃<sub>1</sub>.
Emitted power is proportional to the fourth power of the kelvin temperature, so a ratio of powers is the ratio of temperatures raised to the fourth power.

answer.html: The power per unit area increases by a factor of about 5.1.

check.html: The temperature rose by a factor of 1.5, and the fourth power of 1.5 is a bit more than 5, so the power rises much faster than the temperature.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 3 question: The graph below shows the radiation from a furnace wall at 2000 K. The blue curve is the observed spectrum and the red dashed curve is the prediction of electromagnetic wave theory. Identify the region of the graph where wave theory is a good model of the observed spectrum.

body.html: The graph plots relative intensity against frequency. The observed curve peaks near 1.2 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. We want the frequencies where the two curves agree.
A model is good where its predicted curve lies on top of the measured curve.

The red and blue curves overlap only at the far left of the graph, for frequencies below roughly 0.1 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. By 0.5 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz the red curve has climbed to about twice the observed value and keeps rising steeply, while the blue curve levels off at its peak and then falls.

answer.html: Wave theory works only at very low frequencies, the far left of the graph (below about 0.1 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz).

check.html: A prediction that grows without limit cannot match a real spectrum that comes back down at high frequency, so agreement is only possible at the low-frequency edge.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 4 question: Compare the wavelength of infrared light with the wavelength of visible light, and say what that tells you about the energy of their photons.

body.html: 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆, so photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

Visible light spans about 400 nm to 700 nm. Infrared radiation has wavelengths longer than visible red light (longer than about 700 nm). A longer wavelength means a lower frequency and, from 𝐸= ℎ𝑓= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆, a lower photon energy.

answer.html: Infrared has a longer wavelength than visible light, so each infrared photon carries less energy than a visible-light photon.

check.html: Infrared photons warm things up but cannot cause the chemical changes that ultraviolet photons can, which fits their lower energy.

items.title: Lesson 1, Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Make a two-sided poster. Side 1 shows a feature of light that the wave model explains, and side 2 shows a feature that the particle model explains.

body.html: Use the wave model for diffraction, interference and polarization; use the particle (photon) model for the Compton effect and for how a digital camera sensor detects light.

Sample poster. Side 1, wave model, feature: single-slit diffraction. Light spreads out after it passes through a narrow opening. The pattern is a wide bright central band with dimmer bands on either side, which is what overlapping waves from different parts of the slit would produce. Side 2, particle model, feature: the camera sensor. Each photon with enough energy frees one electron in a pixel. A dim image is built up one photon at a time, as separate dots that add up to the picture. A wave spread smoothly over the sensor could not do this.

answer.html: Sample poster described above: the wave model explains diffraction; the particle model explains how a camera sensor detects individual photons (student drawings will vary).

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Units): Demonstrate that the product of Planck's constant and a frequency, ℎ𝑓, has units of joules.

body.html: ℎ has units of J·s and 1 Hz = 1 / s.

answer.html: Since Hz = s<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>, multiplying by Hz cancels the seconds in J·s and leaves joules, so ℎ𝑓 is an energy.

check.html: This is what we need, because 𝐸= ℎ𝑓 gives the energy of a photon.

items.title: 1: Find the energy, in eV, of a photon of blue light with a wavelength of 448 nm.

body.html: 𝜆= 448 nm; find 𝐸.
Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆.

check.html: 448 nm is blue light, and the blue end of the visible range is near 3 eV, so this fits.

items.title: 2: Find the wavelength of a photon with an energy of 1.65 eV.

body.html: 𝐸= 1.65 eV; find 𝜆.
Rearrange 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆 to 𝜆= ℎ𝑐/ 𝐸.

answer.html: 𝜆= 752 nm (just beyond red, in the near infrared)

check.html: 1.65 eV is below the red end of the visible range (1.8 eV), so the wavelength should be longer than 700 nm.

items.title: 3: Rank these photons from least to greatest energy: (a) 3.4 eV, (b) 275 nm, (c) 905 nm, (d) 2.6 eV.

body.html: Convert every wavelength to energy so that all values are in eV.
275 nm gives 1240 / 275 = 4.51 eV. 905 nm gives 1240 / 905 = 1.37 eV. The others are already in eV: 3.4 eV and 2.6 eV. Order: 1.37 eV < 2.6 eV < 3.4 eV < 4.51 eV.

answer.html: From least to greatest energy: c (905 nm, 1.37 eV), d (2.6 eV), a (3.4 eV), b (275 nm, 4.51 eV).

check.html: The longest wavelength (905 nm) has the least energy and the shortest wavelength (275 nm) has the most.

items.title: 4 (Challenge): The ultraviolet-B band of sunlight runs from 280 nm to 315 nm. Find the range of photon energies in this band.

body.html: 𝜆= 280 nm to 315 nm; find the corresponding energy range.
The shorter wavelength has the greater energy.

answer.html: UV-B photons have energies from about 3.9 eV (315 nm) to 4.4 eV (280 nm).

check.html: These energies are larger than the 1.8 to 3.1 eV of visible photons, as expected for ultraviolet light.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Photoelectric effect): Photons of energy 3.9 eV strike a metal with a work function of 2.2 eV. A student says that every ejected electron leaves with a kinetic energy of 1.7 eV. Explain why some electrons leave with less.

body.html: The work function 𝑊 is the minimum energy to free the most loosely held electron. Other electrons are held more tightly and need more than 𝑊 to escape.

The equation 𝐾𝐸= ℎ𝑓−𝑊= 3.9 eV −2.2 eV = 1.7 eV gives the largest possible kinetic energy. An electron that is deeper in the metal spends extra energy on its way out, so it leaves with less than 1.7 eV.

answer.html: 1.7 eV is the maximum kinetic energy. Electrons bound more tightly use more of the photon's energy to escape, so they leave with less kinetic energy.

items.title: 5: Convert 3.7 eV to joules.

body.html: 𝐸= 3.7 eV; find 𝐸 in J.

answer.html: 5.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J

check.html: One eV is about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J, so a few eV is several times 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J.

items.title: 6: Find the speed of an electron whose kinetic energy is the energy in Problem 5.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸= 5.93 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J, 𝑚= 9.11 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>31</sup> kg; find 𝑣.
𝐾𝐸=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup>

check.html: This is much less than 𝑐= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s, so ordinary (non-relativistic) kinetic energy is fine.

items.title: 7: Find, in eV, the kinetic energy of an electron moving at 3.4 × 106 m/s.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup>, then divide by 1.602 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J/eV.

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸≈33 eV

check.html: This electron is faster than the one in Problem 6 (1.1 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s), so its energy should be more than 3.7 eV, and it is.

items.title: 8: A photocell has a stopping potential of 3.9 V. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in eV.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub> = 𝑒𝛥𝑉<sub>0</sub> (magnitude), so each volt of stopping potential equals one eV of kinetic energy.

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub> = 3.9 eV

check.html: A stopping potential of 1 V stops electrons of 1 eV, so 3.9 V stops 3.9 eV.

items.title: 9: Find, in joules, the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons when the stopping potential is 6.4 V.

answer.html: 1.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>18</sup> J

check.html: 6.4 eV is about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>18</sup> J, consistent.

items.title: 10: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is 6.0 × 10−19 J. Find the stopping potential.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>0</sub> = 3.7 V

check.html: 6.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J is about 3.7 eV, so the stopping potential is 3.7 V.

items.title: 11 (Challenge): A photocell has a stopping potential of 2.6 V. Find the maximum kinetic energy of its photoelectrons in joules.

answer.html: 4.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J

check.html: 2.6 eV is about 4.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> J, consistent.

items.title: 12: A calcium cathode has a threshold wavelength of 423 nm. Find its threshold frequency and its work function in eV.

body.html: 𝜆<sub>0</sub> = 423 nm; find 𝑓<sub>0</sub> (Hz) and 𝑊 (eV).
𝑓<sub>0</sub> = 𝑐/ 𝜆<sub>0</sub> and 𝑊= ℎ𝑓<sub>0</sub> = ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆<sub>0</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>0</sub> = 7.09 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz and 𝑊= 2.93 eV

check.html: Calcium emits electrons for violet light (shorter than 423 nm), and a work function of a few eV is typical.

items.title: 13: Sodium has a work function of 2.36 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected by 380 nm light.

body.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub> = 𝐸<sub>photon</sub> −𝑊.

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub> = 0.90 eV

check.html: The photon energy (3.26 eV) exceeds W (2.36 eV), so electrons are emitted with positive kinetic energy.

items.title: 14: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 254 nm ejects electrons from a metal with a maximum kinetic energy of 1.6 eV. Find the work function of the metal.

body.html: 𝑊= 𝐸<sub>photon</sub> −𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑊= 3.3 eV

check.html: The work function is a few eV, like the metals in Table 1 (magnesium is 3.66 eV), and it is smaller than the photon energy.

items.title: 15 (Challenge): The longest wavelength of light that ejects electrons from a metal surface is 341 nm. Find the work function and use Table 1 (cesium 1.95 eV, magnesium 3.66 eV, silver 4.6 eV, sodium 2.36 eV) to identify the most likely metal.

body.html: The longest wavelength that works is the threshold wavelength, so 𝑊= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆<sub>0</sub>.
Compare with the table: cesium 1.95 eV, sodium 2.36 eV, silver 4.6 eV. Only magnesium (3.66 eV, threshold 339 nm) is close.

answer.html: 𝑊= 3.6 eV; the metal is most likely magnesium.

check.html: 341 nm is very close to magnesium's 339 nm threshold, and no other metal in the table is near.

items.title: Lesson 1, Compton Effect "Get It?": After scattering from an electron, an X-ray photon has a lower frequency than before. Explain what happened to its wavelength and its energy.

body.html: 𝑐= 𝑓𝜆 and 𝐸= ℎ𝑓.
The speed of light 𝑐 is fixed, so a lower frequency means a longer wavelength (𝜆= 𝑐/ 𝑓). Since 𝐸= ℎ𝑓, a lower frequency also means lower energy.

answer.html: The wavelength increased and the photon's energy decreased. The lost energy went to the recoiling electron.

items.title: 16: A very bright red laser cannot eject electrons from a zinc plate, but a dim ultraviolet lamp can. Explain why.

body.html: In the photon model one photon gives its whole energy ℎ𝑓 to one electron. Intensity only changes the number of photons.

Each red photon has less energy than the work function of zinc, so no single red photon can free an electron. The electron cannot save up energy from several photons, so a brighter beam (more photons per second) does not help. Each ultraviolet photon has more than enough energy, so even a dim lamp, with few photons, ejects electrons right away.

answer.html: Ejection depends on the energy of each photon (ℎ𝑓), not on how many photons arrive. Red photons are each too weak, however bright the laser; ultraviolet photons are each strong enough, even when dim.

items.title: 17: A heating element's temperature is raised from 1500 K to 2000 K. What happens to the frequency of its peak intensity and to the total power it radiates?

body.html: A hotter object has its spectrum peak at a higher frequency. The total power is proportional to 𝑇<sup>4</sup>:

answer.html: The frequency of peak intensity increases, and the total radiated power rises by a factor of about 3.2.

items.title: 18: A student studies two experiments. In (i), ultraviolet light shines on a zinc plate and a current is measured. In (ii), 0.050 nm X-rays strike graphite and the scattered X-rays are found to have a longer wavelength. Which experiment shows the photoelectric effect and which shows the Compton effect? Explain.

answer.html: Experiment (i) is the photoelectric effect: each photon is absorbed completely, and its energy goes to the work function plus the kinetic energy of an ejected electron, which gives the current. Experiment (ii) is the Compton effect: the X-ray photon is scattered by an electron and survives with a longer wavelength (less energy and momentum), while the electron recoils.

items.title: 19: A camera's light meter uses a photocell. Explain how a photocell turns light into an electrical signal.

answer.html: A photocell is a device in which photons with at least the threshold frequency free electrons from the material (the photoelectric effect). The freed electrons make a current, and more photons per second means more electrons and a larger current, so the current measures how bright the light is.

items.title: 20: Blue light of wavelength 450 nm gives a stopping potential of 0.95 V. Find the work function of the metal.

body.html: 𝜆= 450 nm, 𝛥𝑉<sub>0</sub> = 0.95 V; find 𝑊 in eV.
𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub> = 𝑒𝛥𝑉<sub>0</sub> = 0.95 eV, and 𝐾𝐸<sub>max</sub> = 𝐸<sub>photon</sub> −𝑊.

check.html: The result is positive and smaller than the 2.76 eV photon energy, as it must be for blue light to eject electrons.

items.title: 21: Find the energy of the photons from a 405-nm blue-violet laser.

check.html: Violet light is near the high-energy end (3.1 eV) of the visible range.

items.title: 22: An X-ray photon scatters from a loosely held electron in a graphite block, and the electron recoils. Compare the frequency of the scattered photon with that of the incident photon.

answer.html: The scattered photon has a lower frequency (and a longer wavelength) than the incident photon, because it gave some of its energy to the recoiling electron and 𝐸= ℎ𝑓.

items.title: 23: A dental X-ray with a wavelength of 0.035 nm is absorbed in tooth enamel and releases an electron. Find the electron's energy in eV. Assume the work function is negligible.

body.html: 𝜆= 0.035 nm, 𝑊≈0; find the electron's energy in eV.

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸≈3.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> eV (about 35,000 eV)

check.html: Dental X-ray photons are tens of keV, which is realistic.

items.title: 24 (Critical Thinking): Use the billiard-ball model for the Compton effect, but suppose the X-ray photon strikes a gold nucleus (thousands of times more massive than an electron) instead of an electron. Would the nucleus gain as much energy as the electron does? Would the scattered photon's wavelength change as much?

body.html: In an elastic collision, a light object bouncing off a much heavier one transfers very little energy to it (like a ping-pong ball hitting a bowling ball).
The heavy gold nucleus barely recoils, so it gains far less energy than the electron did, and the photon loses far less energy. The photon would scatter with almost the same wavelength it had before.

answer.html: No. The nucleus would gain much less energy than the electron, and the scattered photon's wavelength would change by a much smaller amount.

items.title: Module 22 Opener, Encounter the Phenomenon and CER (How could the manipulation of individual atoms be useful in future computing?)

body.html: This is an open-ended claim-evidence-reasoning prompt. Nothing is calculated.

Atoms and electrons obey quantum rules (quantized energies, wave behavior, uncertainty). Because those rules fix the energy levels and positions of individual atoms very precisely, an atom's arrangement or state can act as a stable, tiny, well-defined "bit".

A reasonable claim is "Placing or flipping single atoms lets us store and process information in extremely small spaces." Evidence to collect from this module: (1) energy is quantized, so an atom has distinct, repeatable states (a natural 0 and 1); (2) matter has a de Broglie wavelength of about 0.1 nm for electrons, so atomic-scale structures behave like waves and can be controlled by electric fields; (3) the uncertainty principle sets a limit on how precisely position and momentum can be known, which limits how small and how stable a bit can be. Reasoning: since each atom has predictable energy states and occupies about 0.1 nm, a computer that uses one atom per bit could pack far more data per area than current devices.

answer.html: Sample claim: manipulating individual atoms lets each atom serve as a bit with distinct quantized states, allowing much denser storage and processing. (Student-specific wording will vary.)

items.title: Unit 6 Opener, Ask Questions, Look for Evidence, and STEM Project (What is the universe made of?)

body.html: Open-ended prompts: write questions for the board, record observations in a Summary Table, and investigate "The History of Everything".
These tasks are student-generated and use online resources, so no single numerical result exists. Here is a model response.

Sample questions: What are atoms made of? How do we know what stars are made of? What nuclear reactions release energy? Where did the first atoms come from? Summary Table headings to use for each activity: Activity | Observation | Explanation | Connection to the unit question. Sample entries come from this module: emission spectra show each element has a unique line pattern, so spectra reveal what the universe is made of. For the STEM project, gather evidence such as the cosmic microwave background, the expansion of the universe, abundances of hydrogen and helium, and radioactive dating of rocks, and then write a timeline.

answer.html: Not a computed problem. Sample questions and a Summary Table format are given above; the unit project needs the online resources, so only the method is shown here.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 1 and 2): Explain the changes in the glowing lightbulb as the dimmer control is turned up.

body.html: The dimmer raises the potential difference, so the filament's temperature rises. We need to explain the change in color and brightness.
A hotter object has an emission spectrum that peaks at a higher frequency (Figure 2), and it emits more total power (proportional to 𝑇<sup>4</sup>).

At low temperature the peak is in the infrared, and only the long-wavelength (red) tail of the spectrum is visible, so the bulb is dim and deep red or orange. As the temperature rises, the peak frequency moves up toward the visible range, so yellow and then green, blue and violet are added to the red. When all colors are present in similar strength, the eye sees white. The total power emitted also increases, so the bulb gets brighter.

answer.html: As the filament heats up, the peak of its spectrum shifts to higher frequency (red, to orange, to yellow, to white) and the bulb emits more total power, so it gets brighter.

check.html: This matches Figure 2, where the 8000 K curve peaks at higher frequency and is much taller than the 4000 K curve.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Astronomy Connection): How does the power emitted change if the kelvin temperature is doubled?

body.html: 𝑃∝𝑇<sup>4</sup>. Find 𝑃<sub>2</sub> / 𝑃<sub>1</sub> if 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 2𝑇<sub>1</sub>.
Emitted power is proportional to the fourth power of the kelvin temperature.

answer.html: The power increases by a factor of 16.

check.html: A doubling of 𝑇 gives more than a doubling of power, which fits "hotter objects radiate considerably more."

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 3 question: Identify the region of the graph where electromagnetic wave theory is a good model of the observed spectrum.

body.html: Compare the red dashed (predicted) and blue (observed) curves.

The two curves lie on top of each other only at the far left of the graph, at very low frequencies (below about 0.3 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz, in the infrared). Past that, the predicted curve shoots upward toward infinity while the observed curve peaks near 1.5 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz and then falls.

answer.html: The wave theory works only at very low frequencies (the far left of the graph, roughly below 0.3 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz).

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 4 question: Compare ultraviolet wavelength with visible wavelength and say what that tells you about relative energies.

body.html: 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆, so energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

UV light has wavelengths shorter than visible light (UV is below about 400 nm, visible is about 400 to 700 nm). A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and, from 𝐸= ℎ𝑓= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆 , a higher photon energy.

answer.html: UV has a shorter wavelength than visible light, so each UV photon carries more energy than a visible-light photon.

items.title: Lesson 1, Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): two-sided poster on the wave model and the particle model

body.html: Use the wave model for interference, diffraction and polarization; use the particle (photon) model for the photoelectric effect and the Compton effect.

Sample poster. Side 1, wave model, feature: double-slit interference. Light from two slits overlaps; bright bands appear where crests meet crests (path difference of whole wavelengths) and dark bands where crests meet troughs. Side 2, particle model, feature: photoelectric effect. Each photon has energy ℎ𝑓 and gives all of it to a single electron. If ℎ𝑓 is less than the work function, no electrons are ejected no matter how bright the light is. This explains the threshold frequency and the instant emission.

answer.html: Sample poster described above: wave model explains interference; particle model explains the photoelectric effect (student drawings will vary).

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Units): Demonstrate that J/Hz is equivalent to J·s.

answer.html: Since Hz = s<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>, dividing by Hz is the same as multiplying by s, so J/Hz = J · s.

items.title: 1 (E = 1240 eV·nm/λ): Photon energy for λ = 515 nm

body.html: 𝜆= 515 nm; find 𝐸.
Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆.

check.html: 515 nm is green light, and green photons are about 2.4 eV.

items.title: 2: Wavelength of a 2.03 eV photon

body.html: 𝐸= 2.03 eV; find 𝜆.
Rearrange 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆 to 𝜆= ℎ𝑐/ 𝐸.

answer.html: 𝜆= 611 nm (orange-red light)

check.html: Lower energy than the 2.41 eV photon in Problem 1 gives a longer wavelength, as it should.

items.title: 3: Rank 4.0 eV, 320 nm, 811 nm, 2.1 eV from least to greatest energy

body.html: Convert every wavelength to energy so that all values are in eV.
320 nm gives 1240 / 320 = 3.875 eV ≈3.9 eV. 811 nm gives 1240 / 811 = 1.53 eV. The others are already in eV: 4.0 eV and 2.1 eV. Order: 1.53 eV < 2.1 eV < 3.9 eV < 4.0 eV.

answer.html: From least to greatest energy: c (811 nm, 1.5 eV), d (2.1 eV), b (320 nm, 3.9 eV), a (4.0 eV).

check.html: The longest wavelength (811 nm) has the least energy and the shortest (320 nm) is the highest of the wavelength-given photons.

items.title: 4 (Challenge): Range of photon energies for the visible spectrum (Figure 6)

body.html: Figure 6 shows the visible spectrum from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red).

answer.html: Visible photons have energies from about 1.8 eV (red) to 3.1 eV (violet).

check.html: The short-wavelength end has the greater energy, as expected.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Photoelectric effect): Explain how an ejected electron can have kinetic energy less than the threshold energy.

body.html: ℎ𝑓<sub>0</sub> is the minimum energy to free the most loosely held electron. Other electrons are held more tightly and need more than ℎ𝑓<sub>0</sub> to escape.
Most electrons lose some of the photon's energy getting out of the metal, so they leave with less than the maximum 𝐾𝐸= ℎ𝑓−ℎ𝑓<sub>0</sub>. The equation gives the maximum kinetic energy only.

answer.html: The photon-energy equation gives the maximum kinetic energy. Electrons that are bound more tightly use more of the photon's energy to escape, so they leave with less kinetic energy.

items.title: Lesson 1, Compton Effect "Get It?": Explain why an increase in wavelength indicates a decrease in energy.

body.html: 𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆.
ℎ and 𝑐 are constants, so 𝐸 is inversely proportional to 𝜆. If 𝜆 gets bigger, 𝐸 gets smaller.

answer.html: Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so a longer wavelength means lower energy.

items.title: 16: Why can high-intensity, low-frequency light not eject electrons, while low- intensity, high-frequency light can?

body.html: In the photon model one photon gives its whole energy ℎ𝑓 to one electron. Intensity only changes the number of photons.

Low-frequency photons each have energy less than the work function, so no single photon can free an electron. Many such photons cannot add their energies, because an electron interacts with one photon at a time and cannot store the energy. High-frequency photons each have more than enough energy, so even a few of them eject electrons right away.

answer.html: Ejection depends on the energy of each photon (ℎ𝑓), not on how many photons there are. Low-frequency photons are each too weak, however many arrive; high-frequency photons are each strong enough.

items.title: 18: Distinguish the photoelectric effect from the Compton effect

answer.html: In the photoelectric effect a photon is absorbed completely and ejects an electron from a metal, with the photon's energy going to the work function plus the electron's kinetic energy. In the Compton effect (X-rays, and other very-high-energy photons) the photon is scattered by an electron and survives with a longer wavelength (less energy and momentum), while the electron recoils.

items.title: 19: What are solar cells and how do they work?

answer.html: Solar cells are human-made devices made of semiconductor material that convert light energy into electrical energy. A photon with at least the threshold frequency frees an electron from an atom of the semiconductor, and the freed electrons flow as an electric current in the panel (the photovoltaic effect).

items.title: 24 (Critical Thinking): Billiard-ball model, electron replaced with a much more massive proton

body.html: In an elastic collision, a light object bouncing off a much heavier one transfers very little energy to it (like a ping-pong ball hitting a bowling ball).
The heavy proton barely recoils, so it gains much less energy than the electron did, and the photon loses much less energy. The photon would be scattered with almost the same wavelength.

answer.html: No. The proton would gain much less energy than the electron, and the photon would lose much less energy.
